\boxed{M = \prod_{j=1}^{r} p_j^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}

**Derivation.** Write each number by its exponent vector $\mathbf{i}=(i_1,\dots,i_r)\in\{0,\dots,n\}^r$. A $\gcd$-move takes componentwise minimum, a $\mathrm{lcm}$-move componentwise maximum, so the game is played coordinatewise on the multisets of exponents. In coordinate $j$ each value $k\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ occurs exactly $(n+1)^{r-1}$ times, so there are $N=(n+1)^r$ entries.

For a single-coordinate game with sorted values $x_1\le\cdots\le x_N$, Alice (first, min) makes $a=\lceil(N-1)/2\rceil$ moves and Bob (max) makes $b=\lfloor(N-1)/2\rfloor$ moves. Alice can kill all $a$ values $>x_{b+1}$ by pairing each with a small value: Bob can destroy at most $b$ of the $b+1$ smallest, so one survives for her to use. Dually Bob can kill the $b$ values $<x_{b+1}$ because there are $N-b=a+1$ values $\ge x_{b+1}$ and Alice can remove at most $a$ of them. Hence the value is exactly $x_{b+1}$.

Here $x_{b+1}$ is the $(b+1)$-th smallest exponent. Whether $n=2m$ or $n=2m+1$, a direct count gives $x_{b+1}=m=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Thus Bob can force every coordinate to be $\ge\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ (his moves never consume the large exponents needed to annihilate the small ones), while Alice can force every coordinate to be $\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Consequently the final number is forced to be exactly $\prod p_j^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, which is the minimal $M$ Alice can guarantee.
